point 5. Again, the point of the course is to learn the material, and that may require some digging and experimentation.

Permissible Use of AI Tools

Learning Aid: You may use AI tools to help you understand concepts, generate study notes, brainstorm ideas, and practice skills.

Content Creation: You may use AI to assist with drafting, proofreading, coding, or creating visual elements, provided you disclose this use.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can be a powerful learning assistant when used correctly. When used incorrectly,
it can keep you from the learning and problem solving that will help you in your career.

❌ DO NOT: Use AI to generate answers to the case study questions.

Aside from the fact that this is plagiarism and a violation of the honor code, it also puts you in a
dangerous position. One day, you will sit down for an interview, and your prospective employer might ask,
"Ah, I see you've taken a Software Engineering class. Tell me what your thoughts are on agile development."
or they might ask you to draw out an algorithm on a whiteboard, or explain why a block of code isn't
working. If your default method for solving these types of problems is copy and paste from ChatGPT, you will
not get the job.

The case study questions are designed to help you think deeply about important issues in Software
Engineering. If you have questions about the case study, ask your teammates or your instructor. They are
happy to help.

❌ DO NOT: Use AI to clean up your English.

Many students from outside the United States like to use AI to help them with their English. The problem
here is that nobody in the United States writes or talks like these AI systems, so it becomes very obvious
when someone is doing this. This has become such a problem that many recruiters and hiring managers will
screen cover letters and resumes through AI detectors and throw out the ones that are flagged as likely
written by AI.

If you are afraid that your grammar is poor and you don't have a strong grasp of English, do not worry.
This is not an English class, and you will not be graded on these things.

✅ DO: Ask AI questions to help your understanding.

For example, you might ask: "Please explain what an artifact is in the context of the waterfall method of
software engineering." Or, "What is an after-action report, and why might a company use them?" You would not
want to copy and paste the responses you get from these questions, but you could use them to help you answer
the questions.

Grades in this class are largely based on in-person quizzes and exams, thus improper collaboration
or AI use is not of serious conern. However, my goal is not to catch you at exam times, but
to encourage you to establish good learning habits before that.
Y ou are encouraged to discuss the lecture material, worksheets, handouts and problem sets with
other students. Study groups are highly recommended and very productive by all previous student
reports. However, the only “product” of your discussion should be your memory/understanding
- you should write up solutions individually . Y ou may not exchange written work or computer
files. The group project is the only exception to this - in this case, these collaboration rules apply
to students outside of your group.
Y ou are permitted to use AI-tools or the internet in general, to clarify concepts, to get guidance
on assignments, as long as you do so in an ethical and responsible manner. The bottom line is
you should not use ANY tool to replace your own thinking or analysis. Showing me the correct
answer is never the goal (I know the answers), being able to come up with them yourself is.
Beware however, that it is easy to underestimate the effort it takes. Understanding a solution

AI Tools in CSCI 205

As future software engineers, you need to understand how to effectively use AI tools. However, remember: **AI tools are not replacements for human creativity, originality, and critical thinking.** They are supplements to your learning journey.

## Professional Context

- AI is transforming software development
- You'll be expected to use these tools in your career
- Now is the time to learn their proper place in your toolbox
- Understand their strengths AND limitations

## Allowed Uses

- Debugging assistance
- Code explanations
- Test case generation
- Learning support
- Project work (with attribution)

:::warning
🔑 **Critical Rule:** Never blindly copy code! You MUST understand everything these tools suggest.
:::

## Prohibited Uses

- Quizzes and Progress Checks
- Direct code copying without understanding
- Generating complete solutions
- Avoiding learning fundamentals
- Any use that replaces your own learning

## Attribution Requirements

- Comment your code with AI tool used
- Explain how you modified AI suggestions
- Document what you learned
- Include prompts if significant

## Best Practices

1. Use AI to enhance, not replace, your learning
2. Understand EVERY line of code you submit
3. Build fundamentals before relying on AI
4. Learn to write effective prompts
5. Gauge your own learning - be careful with overreliance

:::danger
🔑 **Important Notes**

- You will have NO access to AI tools during quizzes and progress checks
- These assessments will test YOUR programming and critical thinking skills
- This AI policy is specific to CSCI 205 - other courses may differ

statements.anchor: AI and LLMs may only be used as supplemental learning aids
statements.label: AI only as supplemental aid
statements.passage:
AI tools and Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful resources, and we encourage you to leverage them to support your learning. However, using these tools must not come at the expense of developing your own critical thinking and problem-solving skills. AI and LLMs may only be used as supplemental learning aids, equivalent to a search engine or a 24/7 TA to help clarify concepts. Using AI to generate text, code, or solutions for any homework, lab, quiz, or exam is prohibited. You are solely responsible for ensuring that all submitted work represents your own effort and understanding.

To ensure academic integrity and genuine learning, the instructors reserve the right to require an
in-person code review
for any assignment. Students may also be selected at random or at the instructor’s discretion.

During these reviews, students will be asked to:

Explain the logic behind specific blocks of code.

Discuss why specific libraries or methods were chosen.

Describe how the code would change if certain parameters were altered.

The ability to explain your code is a core requirement for receiving credit.

If a student is unable to fully explain the logic, syntax, or structure of their submitted code, they will receive a
significant grade reduction
.

In cases where a student cannot demonstrate any foundational understanding of the submitted work, a
grade of zero
may be assigned for that project, and the student will be reported for academic misconduct, regardless of whether the code functions correctly or not.

Claude Code and Codex
), GitHub Copilot, built-in IDE extensions (e.g., Cursor, IntelliJ AI Assistant), or any other agentic coding tools are
outright banned
.

You may
ONLY
interact with LLMs and GenAI tools conceptually, and this interaction must take place
exclusively through browser-based chatbots
(such as chatgpt.com or claude.ai).

General Policy

Use LLMs in the same way you might use a friend in the class who is not in your group. You may only use browser-based chatbots to ask high-level, conceptual questions. You must
never
feed your code, skeleton code, or assignment instructions into an LLM, and no LLM-generated code should ever enter your codebase. As a general rule, no code or specific instructions from the course should be pasted, typed, or uploaded into an LLM. If at any point you find yourself stuck on an assignment, concept, or anything else related to CS 61B, we encourage you to find our staff at office hours or lab!

Code Interviews

In order to discourage unacceptable LLM use, we may be conducting random code interviews for all projects.

For students selected for code interviews, we’ll hold short interviews to verify that you are able to explain your code and are capable of generating similar code unassisted.

For more information, please see the
Code Interviews Policy
.

Reasonable Questions (Exclusively via browser-based chatbots)

“What is a garbage collector?”

“What does this mean: Exception in thread “main” java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero”

Absolutely Forbidden
:
These questions/activities will massively detract from your learning experience in the course, and are strictly prohibited:

Allowing any LLM tool, IDE extension, or CLI assistant (e.g., Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, etc.) to access, read, run, or modify your code or repository.

That being said, the use of LLMs in this class is permitted with

, and the below policy applies to all interactions with LLMs relating to CS 61C content:

Reasonable Questions.

Unacceptable Uses of AI/Google/etc

to use AI, Google, etc to complete work on Homework, Projects, and Labs.

will not

summarize the relevant prompts or questions submitted to the tool

identify which parts of the submitted work were influenced by

My understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) and their uses is

statements.passage:
Labs have the same AI policy as your lecture section.

Understanding and using AI are important skills that you will master as part of your CS education at Colby, and the following policy will provide a controlled way for you to use AI to your learning advantage in this course:

Students may use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) solely for understanding concepts, reviewing examples, or receiving feedback on their code. These tools can be valuable for clarifying ideas and enhancing comprehension.

Using AI to generate any code, solutions, or answers is strictly prohibited and considered academic misconduct. All submitted work must be entirely the student’s own effort.

Students must be able to demonstrate their understanding of solutions through verbal explanations, either in class discussions, office hours, or during assessments.

When AI tools are used for understanding concepts, reviewing examples, or receiving feedback related to a specific assignment or project, students must:

Clearly indicate the extent and nature of the AI’s contribution.

Be prepared to discuss and explain the submitted work during office hours or in class

The use of AI code completion tools, such as GitHub Copilot or other similar platforms, is completely prohibited. Students must write and develop their code independently to ensure they are practicing and reinforcing the skills taught in the course.

Here are some examples of prompts that do not violate the AI policy:

“What is the difference between a stack and a queue?”

“How does a binary search tree work?”

“I'm encountering this error message 'IndexError: list index out of range' when running my code. What does it mean, and how can I fix it?”

“Can you explain how Dijkstra's algorithm works? I'm trying to understand its steps and how it’s applied in practice.”

“Can you help me debug my code? Don't generate any code, just help me understand why my code is not working.”

Here are some examples of prompts that violate the AI policy:

“Can you provide me with a solution to this problem?”

“Can you write a function that ...?”

“Can you generate a code snippet that ....?”

“Can you fix my code so that ...?”

Violations of this policy, including the use of AI for generating code or failure to properly document AI interactions, may result in penalties ranging from a warning to a failing grade for the assignment or course, in accordance with the institution's academic integrity policy.

statements.passage:
Effective use of AI has become a core skill in modern computer science and related fields. I encourage you to use AI in this course to build your proficiency. However, with freedom comes responsibility: use AI to enhance your learning, not replace it. You must find balance in your usage so that you learn effectively — this looks different for everyone and requires experimentation.

A primary goal of this course is to prepare you as an AI tool builder. That requires hands-on practice with coding, design, and analysis. If AI does that heavy lifting for you, you have gone too far. Here are a few ideas to guide your AI usage:

Code review:
Write a method yourself, then have AI help you check your work. Make sure you understand any suggestions or fixes the AI proposes. Never accept fixes blindly; your solution may be better aligned with the project goals.

Explore alternative implementations:
Ask AI for more readable or efficient implementations. You might learn about an approach that you did not consider!

Mock quizzes:
Have AI quiz you on concepts, code, or results.

Ultimately, you are responsible for all the code and analyses that you turn in; AI cannot take the blame for shortcomings.
Here are several points to keep in mind:

For base projects, you should only use Python packages listed in
Software
. Do not let AI convince you otherwise.

Be cautious of AI suggestions that involve esoteric or exotic functions or overly complex implementations. If you cannot read and understand them, do not include them!

statements.label: cheating even if cited
statements.passage:
Generative AI systems (like Claude, ChatGPT, etc), if used correctly, can serve as powerful tools for learning and idea refinement. In this course, you can use generative AI systems to learn about concepts iteratively through a conversation (much like you would have a conversation with a peer, TA or an instructor). However, you cannot ask these systems to directly give you answers or write code for you. This is because I believe the intellectual growth you can get from working through a difficult problem and discovering the answer for yourself cannot be replicated by just reading a pre-generated answer — and the skills you learn from this course, such as applying algorithmic reasoning to justify correctness, is more important than ever as AI increasingly lowers the barrier to generating code.

Here are some concrete rules that exemplify this (but are not intended to be comprehensive):

Do NOT:
* Give the model a problem description and ask it to sketch an algorithm for you or write you pseudo code.
* Give the model the homework description and ask it to organize the code for you (e.g., generate the necessary function headers, write the main functions etc).
* Give the model a function description and ask it to generate code for you.
* Given some problem description or code, ask the model to generate test cases for you.
* Use the model to write any aspect of the justification of correctness document.

Using the AI system in ways as described above will count as cheating even if you cite the AI system as a source.

You CAN:
* Ask clarification questions about the fundamentals of programming (e.g., “When should I use a public vs. private method in Java?”)
* Ask for conceptual clarifications (e.g., “What is the difference between average case and best case run times?”)
* Try to work through the logic of something you don’t understand (e.g., “Why is the run time of this algorithm [describe] n^2?”)
* Given a problem description and your proposed algorithm and “talk” through the potential fallacies.

Note, for any of these models having the correct “prompt” is necessary. So you may have varying levels of success using these models to gain conceptual understanding, and in many cases just talking to your instructors/ TA/ peers or even doing straight up googling is likely to yield better results. If you do decide to use these models, it is your responsibility to also fact check the insights that you gain.

External resource policy.
An external resource is anything not provided on the course Canvas page or anyone not part of the course staff. Students may use external resources

. Such resources include books, notes, websites, and AI tools (beware: see the warning below). Students

Students may use tools, including AI tools, for formatting and LaTeX assistance but not for producing the content or wording their solutions.

AI policy.
The AI policy is described in the “external resource policy” above. We warn you that AI tools, as well as some popular websites such as “Geeks for Geeks”, often make mistakes or contain inaccuracies that can be very difficult to detect as a student. You may be learning something incorrectly if you rely on these tools. If you use them, it is best to double-check information with a more reliable source, such as a textbook.

Example: Suppose the homework assignment is: “Prove that binary search makes at most log(n) comparisons.” A student may use an external textbook, website, or AI tool to learn more about how binary search works. However, the student may not search for an answer to the homework problem or a reworded version of it like “how many comparisons does binary search make?”

You may not submit work the work of others and claim it as your own.

This can be the work of other people in the class. This can be the work of
generative AI (e.g. code generated that you did write other than via a
natural language prompt). If you did not do the work yourself, you must be
honest about it, or it is an academic integrity violation. To not disclose this
fact is a form of academic
fraud
.

Note that both sides of the “and” are required for it to be violation. If you
submit work, but are honest who or what was involved in creating it, it is not
an academic integrity violation. Some work of the work that you will do in this
course is expected to be done with other people, so when you submit it your are
not claiming as solely your own.

student that submitted work without properly attributing its source. However,
there is the issue of students that
enable
academic integrity violations.

that work off as their own?

In that case, we will only prosecute for an academic integrity violation if you
were reasonably aware of that the other student would pass if off as their own
work. In that case you are part of a
conspiracy to commit fraud
. This may
sound sinister, but
conspiracy
is just a legal term meaning a plan by two
or more people to do something not permitted. We have more on this in the
section on
preventing violations
below.

AI-based tools such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Code Llama, and others can generate code for you based on natural language prompts that you provide. For this class, I do
not
consider it to be an honor principle violation for
you

short assignment or problem set solutions. However, I strongly urge you to write the solutions yourself, rather than relying on these tools. Most of the true mastery of this course's material happens from striving to create correct and efficient code yourself, not from simply reading and copying an AI-based tool's code. Additionally, these tools will not be available on the midterms and final, so you'll need to fully understand the course material to succeed.

If you choose to use an AI-based tool you
must
:

Cite the tool you used for each method (function) created or debugged with one of these tools, even if you modify the tool-produced code

Be able to explain every line of code in your solution; specifically what the line does and why you included it.

If you choose to use an AI-based tool you
must not
:

Share the prompts you used with anyone (other than your partner, where partners are permitted)

Share the tool's output with anyone (other than your partner, where partners are permitted). Other students must use the tool themselves and must evaluate the tool's output relative to their solution

Use Java-provided classes or methods that we have not discussed in class. Academic integrity is a fundamental aspect of our learning. There might be AI misuse in this

statements.passage:
AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Claude, etc.) can be useful for learning programming concepts, debugging, and practicing problem-solving. In this course, the goal is for
you
to develop the ability to read, write, trace, debug, and explain Java code independently.

You may use AI tools to:

Ask for explanations of Java concepts, syntax, errors, or compiler messages.

Request examples that are
not
copied into your assignment.

Brainstorm
approaches
to a problem before writing your own solution.

Get
hints
for debugging after attempting the problem yourself.

Study
for quizzes and exams.

You may not:

Submit code written wholly or in part by an AI tool as your own work.

Ask an AI tool to complete an assignment, lab, homework, or project for you.

Copy AI-generated code, comments, variable names, or test cases into a submission.

Use AI tools during quizzes, exams, or other assessments designated as closed-resource.

If you use an AI tool while working on an assignment, include a brief note at the beginning of your submission, after your honor code statement:

/*AI Use Statement: I used [tool name] to [e.g., explain a compiler error / review my approach / suggest debugging steps]. I wrote and tested all submitted code myself.*/

If you did not use AI, write:

/*AI Use Statement: No AI tools were used.*/

You should be prepared to explain how your program works, trace your code on a small example, and modify or extend your solution during class, office hours, or a follow-up discussion. Inability to explain or modify submitted work may be treated as evidence that the submission is not your own.
Violations of this policy will be handled according to the course's Academic Honest policy (see above).

The goal of this policy is to encourage you to use AI responsibly -- to augment your own learning rather than circumvent it.

statements.label: students should use AI
statements.passage:
Use of AI Tools Policy – Coding Tasks
We recognize that students will use AI - that they should use AI, as almost everyone
in industry is encouraged and/or forced to do so. Our goal for students is to teach how
to use AI more effectively than others to empower you to succeed in projects and
work. In short, we allow the use of AI in the context of writing code for those
assignments and projects in which we explicitly say so . We will have three levels
concerning the use of AI for coding assignments and projects:
1. AI encouraged: The student can use any and all AI assistance as they desire.
Please note that, at this level, the instructional team reserves the right to ask
for proctoring and supervising mechanisms to ensure significant learning: i.e.,
worklogs, videos, prompt transcripts, etc.
2. AI permitted: The student can use AI for coding assignments and projects, but
must use it under the “Use of AI Tools Policy - Non-code Tasks” guidelines.
Additional constraints may apply per assignment or project, considering our
instructional team’s criteria.
3. AI limited: The student must not use any AI to complete the assignment.
AI removes the need for intimate understanding of every programming language you
work in and expedites development. The trade-off for this is three primary risks:
1. Stuck when debugging. Often, students end up in a spot where the code
doesn’t work, but are unsure why; before when students wrote all of their
code, debugging was much more intuitive and smoother because designers
possessed a strong understanding of the system being developed because
every step of the process was understood. Now with generative AI, students
lose this intimate understanding.
2. Incorrect/inefficient approach. AI is prone to developing code in an
inefficient or incorrect way when it lacks the context of the entire project. E.g.
Asking AI to develop a filtering system on a list view page, but not telling the
AI that there will be images involved in the future therefore lacking robustness
in the solution.
3. Reduced learning. Quite simply, the more you rely on AI to write for you
rather than with you, the less you will ultimately learn. AI should be treated
as scaffolding: something that supports your growth, not something that
replaces the work you must do to develop your own skills. In much the same
way, when you go to a gym, the more you depend on assistance to reduce the
rigor of your training, the less meaningful and effective that workout becomes.
Growth

statements.passage:
Artificial Intelligence & Academic Honesty
We treat AI-based assistance, such as but not limited to ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude, and Gemini,
the same way we treat collaboration with other people: you are welcome to talk about your ideas
and work with other people, both inside and outside the class, as well as with AI-based
assistants.
However, all work you submit must be your own. You should never include in your assignment
anything that was not written directly by you without proper citation (including quotation marks
and in-line citation for direct quotes).
Including anything you did not write in your assignment without proper citation will be treated
as an academic misconduct case. If you are unsure where the line is between collaborating with
AI and copying AI, we recommend the following heuristics:
1. Heuristic 1: Never hit “Copy” within your conversation with an AI assistant. You can
copy your own work into your own conversation, but do not copy anything from the
conversation back into your assignment. Instead, use your interaction with the AI
assistant as a learning experience, then let your assignment reflect your improved
understanding.
2. Heuristic 2: Do not have your assignment and the AI agent open at the same time. Similar
to the above, use your conversation with the AI as a learning experience, then close the
interaction down, open your assignment, and let your assignment reflect your revised
knowledge. This heuristic includes avoiding using AI directly integrated into your
composition environment: just as you should not let a classmate write content or code
directly into your submission, so also you should avoid using tools that directly add
content to your submission.
Deviating from these heuristics does not automatically qualify as academic misconduct;
however, following these heuristics essentially guarantees your collaboration will not cross the
line into misconduct.

You may not use these tools to summarize readings, generate discussion points, write reading journals, write code, or as any other type of resource.

You are always responsible for the full authorship and accountability for your work. Misrepresenting the output of other people as your own original work is a serious breach of academic integrity standards.

Where does AI fit?
As noted above, LLMs are an industry-expected toolset for helping create software source-code. That said, there are students who do not want to use AI or who constrain their AI use in a variety of ways. It is possible to thrive in CS5 without AI at all (many generations of students have done so!), and you are welcome not to use it. You are also welcome to use it under constraints of your choosing -- chat with the instructor(s) if you have concerns about this.
(Within the
HMC AI-use guidelines
, cs5's AI-use score is student-chosen, between perhaps a
0.42
and
4.2
. That is, prompt-space is
never required

part of the curriculum
itself

It's also true that a growing subset of professional paths expect sophistication with computing and AI
together
. For example, applied computer science -- even far from software-engineering or software-centric roles -- seeks

source-code and software
control

(the ability, just-in-time, to change artifacts in order to match your and others' newly intended behaviors)
and

source-code and software
communication

(the ability to convey the underlying mechanisms-of-operation to others, and to yourself)
--

source-code and software
accountability

(vouching for and demonstrating the ability to handle expected and unexpected behavior in one's software systems)
--

These three skills are
more
valuable than ever,
because they no longer always get the "free-ride" that comes when source is
personally
generated!

To serve as wide an audience as possible
, cs5 encourages the development of these professionally and personally valuable skills (including the use of AI -- for those interested in honing their skills with it).

statements.passage:
In all respects, using AI (such as ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot) is equivalent to turning to a friend who has already taken the class and asking them for help—the same rules apply. It would not be okay to have a friend do your homework for you, or sit next to you telling you at each moment what to write next.

The AI usage rules below are thus just a restatement of the general principles above, with a focus on how they apply to AI tools.

Your Responsibilities

Unlike other sources of help who may naturally exercise their own good judgment in deciding what information to provide, you may need to take explicit steps to prevent AI tools and assistants from inadvertently providing you with answers or solutions that you should be developing on your own. For example, Visual Studio Code makes it very easy to turn on GitHub Copilot and receive suggestions for code completions, causing AI to write code that was supposed to be your own work. It is your responsibility to ensure that you can tell whether AI code completions are enabled or not and ensure that they are
disabled
while working on code for this class.

Likewise, if you ask an AI assistant such as ChatGPT a question about assignment materials or code, there is a good chance that the assistant will be too direct in giving you solutions, giving you an unfair advantage over your classmates, undermining your own learning process, and potentially violating the Honor Code. One way to avoid such issues is to avoid using AI assistants for direct help with assignments or code (conceptual discussions about lesson materials would be okay). Talking to a grutor or your professor, or posting your about your issue on Piazza, will avoid these kinds of challenges.
